title: The sun is a morning star
word: The sun is a morning star
hook: the sun is but a morning star; there is more day to dawn (Walden 18)

segments.voice: Yesterday, give me truth: rather than love, money or fame, and a rich table Thoreau left hungry. Where did you say the true thing? Day one thousand two hundred forty-four.

A kitchen table, old and plain, made of apple-tree wood. It has stood in a farmhouse for years. Meals, elbows, spilled milk. And one day the family hears a gnawing sound inside it. Then a bug chews its way out of the dry wood into the room, alive and beautiful. Thoreau tells this story on the last pages of Walden. The egg, the story goes, had been laid in the living tree long before the tree became a table, and it waited all that time. He tells it as a little resurrection, life coming out of dry wood. And then he ends the whole book with a few short sentences about the dawn.
screen: `AN OLD APPLE-WOOD TABLE.` → `A GNAWING SOUND.` → `LIFE OUT OF DRY WOOD.`

segments.voice: Here are the last lines of Walden, in Thoreau's own words: "The light which puts out our eyes is darkness to us. Only that day dawns to which we are awake. There is more day to dawn. The sun is but a morning star." Four sentences. Take them one at a time. First, too much light. A light bright enough to blind you is, to you, the same as dark. Some truths arrive too big to see all at once. Second, the day you're awake for. A sunrise happens whether you notice or not. But Thoreau says only that day dawns to which we are awake. The calendar can say morning while a person is still asleep inside. A real dawn needs someone awake for it. Third, more day to dawn. This is the turn. After a whole book of mornings at the pond, he says the day isn't finished arriving. There's more of it coming. Fourth, the sun is but a morning star. A morning star is the bright point you see before sunrise, a sign that the day is near. Thoreau takes the sun itself, the biggest light we have, and calls it that: only a sign of a brighter day still on its way. It's a strange, hopeful way to end a book. Not with a summary. Not with a moral. With a sunrise demoted to a herald, and the bug in the table still fresh in mind: life that waited in dry wood, and came out when it was ready.
screen: `LIGHT THAT PUTS OUT OUR EYES.` · `ONLY THE DAY WE'RE AWAKE TO.` · `MORE DAY TO DAWN.` · then, large: `THE SUN IS BUT A MORNING STAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch the dawn. If it's morning, turn toward the east, a window or a doorway will do, and watch the light as it is right now. If it's another hour, find the brightest light in reach, a window, a lamp, the sky, and sit with it, or remember one dawn you were actually awake for. Settle and breathe. Don't look straight at the sun. Just notice the light changing, or holding still. And let the line sit underneath your breath: there is more day to dawn. The bell holds the time.
The sun is a morning star. Thoreau's last image in Walden: even the sun is only a sign of a bigger day still coming. Today's word.
screen: `THE SUN IS A MORNING STAR — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: more day to dawn. Today, at one moment that feels finished, a long task or a tired evening, ask what part of the day you haven't been awake for yet. Day one thousand two hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Readers often return to the last lines of Walden as a morning reading: a reminder to be awake for the day that is actually arriving, and that more of it is still to come.
